accuracy.evidence: Messages checked against DfE statutory guidance Relationships Education, RSE and Health Education (2019, 'Being safe': each person's body belongs to them; it is not always right to keep secrets if they relate to being safe; how to ask for advice or help and keep trying until they are heard), the NSPCC Talk PANTS rules (your body belongs to you, no means no, talk about secrets that upset you, speak up and someone can help) and the EYFS statutory framework ELG Managing Self / PSED. The lost-in-a-shop advice (stay inside, go to a staff member at the till or a parent with children, say your name) matches common police and NSPCC lost-child guidance; the lab deliberately avoids teaching that every unknown adult is dangerous and instead teaches who to approach. No frightening detail is given; examples stay at hurt knees, pushing, tickling, unwanted kisses and 'do not tell' secrets.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented barriers to disclosure and help-seeking in young children (NSPCC 'Letting the Future In' and PANTS guidance; DfE guidance on keeping trying until heard): believing a friendly or smiling stranger is trusted (step 1 prediction, card 'someone I do not know', tag stranger, p1), fear of being in trouble or 'telling tales' (tag hide, m1, m8), running outside or hiding when lost (step 3 prediction, shop spots 'go outside to look' and 'hide behind the shelf', tags leave and hidden, p2), thinking you must accept an unwanted hug or kiss (step 4 prediction about Grandpa, m2), keeping a secret because an adult said so (step 5, tag secret, p4, m7 for the surprise contrast) and giving up after one busy adult (step 6, tag giveup, m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtrust is built around this topic's own safety plan: a five-finger helping hand that is filled with trusted adults and then reused in 'Keep telling', a tell-or-OK sort, a shop scene with safe and unsafe choices when lost, three say-no moments about the child's own body, a surprise-versus-worry-secret sort, and a persistence step where the first adult is busy. It differs from flagsafe (Rules that keep us safe: roads, running, hot things), flagcare (everyday kindness) and flagcalm (calming strategies). The gate reports under 30% shingle overlap with every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner acts first and the feedback states the rule: tapping 'someone I do not know' gives 'You do not know them, even if they smile', so a trusted adult is defined by knowing them; sorting six moments shows that hurt, pushed, worried and lost all go to 'Tell a grown-up'; in the shop, the door and the shelf each explain why they are wrong, and finding two helpers prompts 'Tell them your name and your grown-up's name'; choosing 'Kiss her anyway' explains body ownership; in Keep telling the first adult says 'Not now' and only a second try gets help.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each have a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves. 'Yes, she smiled' fails when the unknown person cannot go on the hand. 'Run outside to look' fails when the exit spot says to stay inside because your grown-up will look for you there. 'No, I have to' (hug Grandpa) fails when the say-no moments accept 'No thank you and wave' and explain that your body belongs to you. The task-done line echoes the learner's locked-in choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; each wrong option carries a tag with its own message: hide (you will not be in trouble, tell so they can help), leave (stay inside the shop), hidden (if you hide no one can find you), quiet (say 'Stop!' in a big voice and tell), hit (hitting or shouting can hurt, use words and get help), secret (a secret that makes you feel bad is a worry secret), giveup (keep telling until a grown-up listens) and stranger (a smile or sweets does not make someone safe).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes the learner limits; the adult text was rewritten in shorter sentences after the first check read it at FK 12.9, and now passes the 9.5 limit. Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (hurt, worried, lost, busy). Lab step text is two or three short sentences meant to be read aloud by a grown-up, and canvas labels are a few words ('Tell a grown-up', 'All OK', 'mum with children').

no_filler.evidence: No filler pattern matches. Each step does one job (who is trusted, when to tell, lost in a shop, saying no, secrets, persistence). Feedback lines say exactly what to do instead, and item explanations give the reason in one or two sentences rather than repeating the prompt.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px in light and dark and at 1200 px desktop were taken for every step before and after Show me. The six people cards and the four shop spots are large tap targets (about 110 × 60 px and 160 × 115 px on a phone) and sit clear of the feedback banner. After the first screenshots the hand was fixed (finger number labels had left the palm filled dark brown) and the card and shop figures were shrunk so their labels no longer touch the drawings. The young style gives 56 px buttons below the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas tap has a button: one per person (aria-label 'Put Mum on my hand'), 'Tell a grown-up / All OK', each shop choice, both say-no options, 'Surprise: OK for now / Worry secret: tell', and one per hand name in Keep telling (aria-label 'Tell Gran'). After every move the canvas aria-label reads the last feedback and the current state, e.g. 'You are lost in a shop. Safe helpers found: 1 of 2.' Challenge feedback is an aria-live status. walk.cjs reports axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors; in dark mode the canvas keeps a light card so drawings keep their contrast.
